title: The Goddess Brighid
author: Ancient
content:
The Goddess Brighid

by Wendy M. Reynolds

Note: The information contained on this page has been entirely found on
the web.
It by no means claims to be a comprehensive study of Brighid.

Introduction to Brighid

Traditionally, the formalized study of mythology explores the classical
myths
of Greek and Roman ancestry. Oftentimes, in the academic arena, mythology, 
from any
period other than ancient, goes unresearched and understudied. In the
Middle Ages,
local mythology was the "religion" of the time. In the early
part of the
medieval period, Europe was not yet Christianized; the worship of pagan
and
mythological figures was everywhere. Following Europe's conversion to
Christianity,
people had a hard time letting go of their beloved pagan figures and often
gave a
pagan figure a Christian name. This is the case of the pagan goddess, and
converted
Christian saint, Brighid.

Brighid is an interesting case because she holds such a strong
following in both
the pagan and Christian period. Mythologists and historians alike
believe that since Brighid was such a loved figure 
she was converted
into a Christian saint. Though Brighid was one of the most popular
goddesses,
like many mythologies throughout Europe in the Middle Ages, easily
accessible information
on Brighid is hard to find. So, who is the pagan goddess of the Middle
Ages? Why
was she so beloved and revered? What remnants of her traditions continue
to exist?
What is her role in the modern sense? And, why, if she was so beloved in
so many
different cultures, is there such little information available on her in
Christianity?
What relevancy does she hold to literary study of the Middle Ages? I will
attempt to
begin to uncover some of the mysteries of Brighid, and try to re-create a
history
that is now only scattered.

Who is Brighid?

Brighid is a goddess found in many mythologies including those of
Ireland, France,
and Wales. Because she exists in so many different cultures, Brighid has
literally 
a never ending list of 
names
.
Derived from the Gaelic words Breo-Saighit, her name means "fiery
arrow".
Brighid is often symbolized by fire, flames, and the hearth; she is also
symbolized
by water (cauldrons), grain (Brigid wheels, Brigid's Bed), creatures (a
white cow
with red ears and swan) and also by talismans (spinning wheel).

Brighid is best known and written about in the context of Celtic
mythology.
In Celtic mythology, Brighid is the goddess of inspiration, smithcraft,
and healing. Perhaps Brighid was so popular in pagan tradition because of
her status as a 

triple
goddess
. In the realm of inspiration,
Brighid oversees poets, poetry, creativity, prophecy, and the arts; in
smithcraft
she oversees blacksmiths, goldsmiths, and household crafts; and in
healing, Brighid
looks after healers, medicine, spiritual healing, and fertility (crops,
land, cattle).

Though best known as Brighid, another significant name for her
is Ceridwen. Ceridwen is Brighid's name in Welsh folklore. Ceridwen holds
an incredibly
important role as a mythological and historical figure because she is said
to be the mother
of the famous Welsh poet, Taliesin. Although Ceridwen and Brighid have
separate
histories the only difference comes from the separate cultures. Brighid,
unless
otherwise specified, refers also to Ceridwen.

This excerpt from 
"Brighid"

is a further explanation of who she is:

She is the 'Lady of the Shores', for the shore is one of those
magical in-between
        places that so fascinated the Celts. These in-between places such
as shorelines,
        fords, doorways and so on, were neither one state nor the other.
The shore is neither
        dry land, nor is it the sea, yet it is the meeting place of both.
If we consider
        that the land represents our solid, material world, while the sea
represents the
        Great Cosmic womb of all life, the intuitive side of our nature,
we can see that
        the shore is a meeting place between one world and another.

        Brighid is also known as the 'Two-Faced One'. In the legends she
is described as
        having one side of her face black and ugly, and the other white
and beautiful. The
        Mystery of Bride is to be found in the annual transformation of
the cailleach, the
        hag of winter, into the fair maiden of Spring.

        Brighid is the goddess of all arts and crafts, and as such she is
the feminine principle
        of the Ildanach, the counterpart of Lugh Lamhfada. She represents
the potential of
        all women for she is the eternal flame that burns in the heart and
hearth of every
        woman of the Gael, 'moon-crowned Brighid of the undying flame'.
This principle of
        the undying flame continued even after the coming of Christianity
into Ireland. At
        the fifth century sanctuary of St. Bride of Kildare, the sacred
fire within was attended
        by her devoted maidens and was never allowed to go out. "

        Finally, as the Good Shepherdess who watches over her flock,
Brighid presides over
        the cradle of the new born infant. It is a common practise for the
women of the Isles
        to hang rowan crosses over their cradles whilst reciting a charm
or prayer to Brighid
        to invoke her protection. Yes, Brighid is still loved and revered
by the Gaelic peoples
        of Scotland and Ireland. Long may it continue.

Brighid and her stories

There are several stories about Brighid regarding her history and who
she was.
Most often, she is said to be the daughter of 
Dagda
,
but this is disputable. Miriam Harline discusses this issue in 
"Brighid's
Fires Burn High
:

 Celtic lore makes Brighid the daughter fo the Dagda, the Good
God, and marries
        her to Bres of the Fomors, by whom she bears a son Ruadan. But, as
Janet and Stewart
        Farrar write in the The Witches' Goddess, 'The fact that Dana,
though goddess/ancestress
        of the Tuatha, is sometimes referred to (like Brighid) as the
Dagda's daughter; the
        hints... that the Dagda was orignially the son of this primordial
goddess, then her
        husband, then her father; the dynastic marriage between Brighid
and Bres--all these
        reflect a long process of integration of the pantheons of
neighboring tribes, or
        of conquerors and conquered, and also of patriarchalization.' Like
many goddesses,
        Brighid probably once birthed the god later called her father.

Although there is specualtion about Brighid's personal story, two
stories
remain the most common. In one story, she is the wife of 
Bres

and the mother of Ruadan who fought in the second battle of Magh Tuireadh
and was
killed. Brighid went to the battlefield to mourn her son. Later this was
said to
be the first keening (it has been a tradition in Ireland, until recently,
to hire
women to 
caim

at every graveside). Another story has Brighid as the wife of Tuireann and
the mother
of three sons: Ircharba, Iuchar, and Brian. (Her sons killed the father of
a god when
he was in the form of a pig.)

Perhaps more famous stories exist about the children, of
Ceridwen.
The story of Ceridwen's Cauldron seems to be more widely known than the
stories
of the
same goddess called Brighid. The 
tale
of Ceridwen
 is told in two versions. One story tells the myth
Ceridwen and another
tells the 
tale
of Taliesin
. Interestingly enough, Taliesin's story is significantly
longer than
that of Ceridwen's, although it is basically the same story--the story of
Taliesin's
birth.

Apart from the stories of her children, several stories concerning
Brighid have shaped many different traditions. We are able to know
many of these
stories because Brighid is still worshipped and revered
throughout the
world. These stories include 
Making
Bride's Bed
, 
Brighid
the Midwife
, 
Augury
in Brighid's Name
, 
Imbolc
Spells and Workings
, and the amusing and farsical 
Apocryphal
History of Saint Brighid of the Log
.

Brighid in the Christian tradition

When Europe converted to Christianity, some of the pagan goddesses and
gods continued
to be worshiped, and some were brought into the Christian tradition.
Brighid is one
of those figures whom the people adopted into Christianity. According to

"Brigit
of the Celts"
, "Brigit is the best example of the survival
of a Goddess
into Christian times. She was coannonized by the Catholic church as St.
Brigit and
various origins are given to this saint." St. Brigit is often said to
have been
the midwife of Christ and a close friend to Mary.

In 
Candlemas
Customs & Lore
, Selena Fox gives additional insight into the
Christianized
Brighid:

 When Ireland was Christianized, veneration of the Pagan
Goddess Brigid was
        transformed into that of St. Brigit, said to be the human daughter
of a Druid. St.
        Brigit became a saint after her "death" and was
supposedly converted and
        baptized by St. Patrick. Pagan lore was incorporated into the
Christian traditions
        and legends associated with Her as a saint. For example, as St.
Brigit, She had the
        power to appoint bishops and they had to be goldsmiths. She was
associated with miracles
        and fertility. Into the 18th century a women's only shrine was
kept to her in Kildare
        (meaning Church of the Oak) in Ireland. There, nineteen nuns
tended Her continually
        burning sacred flame. An ancient song was sung to Her: 'Brigid,
excellent woman,
        sudden flame, may the bright fiery sun take us to the lasting
kingdom.' Brigid/St.
        Brigit was said to be the inventor of whistling and of
keening.

Though Celtic tradition especially loved and preserved her,
Brighid's
name and stories are not found within Christianity, specifically the
Catholic
tradition
today. Instead, people outside of Christian tradition have again adopted
Brighid
and she is the focus of their worship.

Modern Worship of Brighid

In Celtic mythology and lore, as well as in other mythologies, the
stories of
Brighid remain alive. However, the formal worship of Brighid today, is
primarily
within wiccan and goddess worshiping circles. There has in fact been, in
the last
few years, a strong resurgence of Brighid. History reports that 
nuns at Kildare always protect Brighid's sacred flame. This shrine was
destroyed, but
has been re-instated in Ireland. Today, people can again see the eternal
flame of
Brighid burning.

 Several things have recently been written to and about
Brighid
in goddess worshipping circles. A universal saying is the 
charge
of the goddess
. The "Charge of the Goddess," however, is not
restricted
to Brighid,
but through it we can see Brighid's parallels in goddesses of other
cultures.

Specific invocations also exist to Brighid; the following is
from 
CelDara:
The Brigit Page
:

Invocation to Brigit

Brigit, Wise One, We, your children, call to you. Lady,
Smithy, We, your children,
        invite you here. Triple Goddess, We, your children, ask your
presence. Brigit, Wise
        One, We, your children, call to you. Lady, Smithy, We, your
children, invite you
        here. Triple Goddess, We, your children, ask your presence.
Brigit, Wise One, We,
        your children, call to you. Lady, Smithy, We, your children,
invite you here. Triple
        Goddess, We, your children, ask your presence, NOW.

The Goddess and Literature

Goddesses have been a part of literature and literary tradition since
the beginning of writing. Most often, male author's incorporate the female
goddess into 
their text. 
The Poet
and
the Goddess

examines the phenomena of goddesses in poetry. Interestingly enough, the
poets cited
include Homer, Geoffrey Chaucer, and Percy Shelley. The poet Robert Graves
said "the
function of poetry is the religious invocation of the Muse; its use is the
experience
of mixed exaltation and horror that her presence excites..." Why is
the goddess
such a central force in poetry?

Brighid was the goddess of poetry and inspiration; why is she the
inspiration
to male poetry. Until very recently, in the context of human existence,
the poets recognized
and taught are male. Brighid (Ceridwen) herself was said to be the mother
of one
of the most famous Welsh poets, Taliesin. Why is it the son and not the
mother? Could
it be that perhaps some of the poetry attributed to male authors could
have been
female?

Because we presume myths as fact,
it is reasonable that what has been written could have been written by a
woman.
This,
of course, is only an assertation based on questions. But, I feel that it
must be
considered that in the case of "tales" that women could be the
authors.

In the case of Taliesin, it is Taliesin and his father, Gwion, that are
written
about. Ceridwen is the person in the "family" who represents
poetry, wisdom,
and inspiration; yet she is rarely written about alongside Taliesin.

Conclusion

Brighid has been a part of many cultures since the beginning of, and
possibly before,
the Middle Ages. Her universal appeal as the goddess of inspiration,
healing, and
smithcraft, led to her prominent status in the mythologies of various
countries and
cultures. She was such a beloved figure that she was converted into a
Christian figure.
Although she has many different faces, now information on her is scarce.
Although
one may only need to search for one name with many figures, Brighid
illudes us. Her
many names and her varied history do not lend to an easy study of
her. However, a good deal of information on Brighid exists on the web and
otherwise--it's
simply a matter of finding it.

As the goddess of poetry and inspiration, Brighid serves poets well for
inspiration
(as Graves says.) But, is there a possiblity that
Brighid was not
only a source of inspiration but actually a poet herself? Of course, there
is no way, to know this, but it is a valid question.

Brighid has gone through many different phases in her
"existence," and
there seems to be a revitalization of Brighid going on. The re-lit flame
at Kildare
is one symbol of Brighid that was previously exstinquished, but has been
brought back.
It is a true testament to her importance that this medieval goddess has
and continues
to be remembered throughout the world.
